title: Labour-market change is making social-protection coverage, adequacy, and financing a central resilience question
source_unit: ILO, Universal social protection in changing labour markets: Protecting workers in all types of employment
geography: Global labour markets and country experiences used by the ILO policy paper

observations.period: 2026 policy paper; current and emerging labour-market conditions

denominator.unit: global social-protection system and labour-market policy frame; no single survey denominator

coverage_gap.value: Persistent gaps in social-protection coverage leave categories of workers and the population at large less protected against social risks

adequacy_gap.value: Coverage alone is insufficient where benefits do not provide adequate protection through labour-market and life-course transitions

priority_worker_groups.value: Temporary, part-time, self-employed, domestic, agricultural, micro- and small-enterprise, and workers in complex employment arrangements are highlighted as groups often facing protection gaps

observations.method: The ILO policy paper synthesizes international social-security standards, country experiences, labour-market analysis, and policy options for extending universal protection across employment types and life-course risks.
observations.uncertainty: This is a policy synthesis rather than a harmonized prevalence estimate. Country experiences are not automatically comparable, and the paper does not identify the size of every coverage or adequacy gap in a common denominator.
observations.subgroup: Workers in non-standard, informal, self-employed, domestic, agricultural, micro-enterprise, and platform-like or complex employment arrangements, plus households facing illness, unemployment, parenthood, disability, old age, climate, or other shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some contributory systems are deliberately targeted and can be adequate for covered workers; universal systems can also create fiscal and administrative tradeoffs. The paper presents expansion and coordination as policy tasks, not proof that one design fits all economies.

observations.period: 2026 policy paper; adaptation to climate, demographic, technological, and structural transformation

denominator.unit: social-protection financing and resilience framework described by the ILO

financing_route.value: Social-security contributions and progressive taxation are identified as core financing routes, complemented where needed by public subsidies for workers with limited contributory capacity

transition_support_route.value: Protection systems can support transitions between jobs, sectors, and forms of employment and across parenthood, unemployment, illness, disability, and old age

resilience_route.value: Robust systems are described as buffers that help workers and enterprises adapt to climate, technology, demographic, and other shocks while reinforcing social cohesion

observations.method: The paper connects social insurance, tax financing, subsidies, labour-market policy, and international solidarity into a systems framework for resilience and decent work.
observations.uncertainty: The source describes plausible institutional mechanisms and country lessons, not a cross-country causal estimate of benefit receipt on resilience, consumption, employment, or political trust.
observations.subgroup: Workers and enterprises moving through employment transitions, governments financing social protection, social partners, and households exposed to economic, climate, health, demographic, or technological shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Contribution-based financing can strengthen risk sharing and accountability, while subsidies and international support can widen inclusion; each route has administrative, fiscal, and political constraints that determine actual reach.

boundary: This record adds institutional coverage, adequacy, financing, transition, and resilience mechanisms. It is not respondent-level data, does not estimate benefit take-up or household effects, and does not establish causal effects of social protection on work, consumption, health, or political behavior.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO publication and news pages retrieved; the paper's coverage, adequacy, target-worker, financing, transition, and resilience mechanisms were cross-checked against the official descriptions. The local hash is for the official publication-page capture, not a claimed local PDF copy.
